all.name: Comparison Model and Lower Bounds
all.description: Studies the comparison model where items are only compared pairwise, using decision trees to derive the worst-case lower bound for comparison-based search.

all.name: Direct Access Arrays
all.description: Covers using integer keys as array indices for constant-time operations, and why this becomes impractical when the key universe is large.

all.name: Hashing and Hash Functions
all.description: Explains mapping large key spaces into smaller hash tables using hash functions, including division hashing and universal hashing families.

all.name: Collision Resolution and Chaining
all.description: Describes handling hash collisions by storing colliding items in chains, and how load factor determines expected operation time.

all.name: Priority Queues and Binary Heaps
all.description: Introduces the priority queue interface and implements it with binary heaps stored as implicit complete trees, supporting insert and delete-max.

all.name: Heap Sort and Heap Construction
all.description: Covers using priority queues to sort, in-place heap sort, and linear-time heap building.

all.name: Balanced Trees for Priority Queues and Sets
all.description: Compares AVL-tree implementations of sets, multisets, and sequences against array-based priority queue approaches.

all.name: Dynamic Programming Foundations
all.description: Introduces dynamic programming via subproblem definition, the SRT BOT steps, and subproblem constraints and expansion.

all.name: Classic Dynamic Programming Problems
all.description: Applies dynamic programming to longest common subsequence, longest increasing subsequence, and the alternating coin game.

all.name: Sample Exam Practice
all.description: Practice problems from Quiz 1 to test understanding across hashing, heaps, and dynamic programming topics.

notes_section.title: Key Concepts
notes_section.text:
**Comparable items.** The lecture models items as *comparable items*: black boxes that support only comparisons between pairs. The allowed comparisons are $<$, $\le$, $>$, $\ge$, $=$, and $\neq$. Each comparison returns a binary result, True or False. The algorithm cannot look inside an item, hash it, or use its bits.

**Goal of the model.** Store a set of $n$ comparable items and support a `find(k)` operation. Since the algorithm can only compare, its running time is bounded below by the number of comparisons it performs. So the useful thing to count is comparisons.

**Decision tree.** Any algorithm can be drawn as a decision tree of the operations it performs. For a comparison algorithm:
- An **internal node** is a binary comparison, with one branch for True and one for False.
- A **leaf** is termination, and it gives the algorithm's **output**.
- A **root-to-leaf path** is one execution of the algorithm on some input.

**Leaves and outputs.** Every possible output needs at least one leaf. A search over $n$ items can return any of $n$ found positions or report that the key is absent, so it needs at least $n+1$ distinct outputs. That means at least $n+1$ leaves.

**The chain of inequalities.** The lecture states:

$$\text{running time} \;\ge\; \#\text{comparisons} \;\ge\; \text{max length of any root-to-leaf path} \;\ge\; \text{height of tree}$$

The first inequality holds ...

quiz_questions.question_text: In the comparison model, a search over a set of $n$ comparable items must produce a decision tree with at least how many leaves?
quiz_questions.explanation:
## Why $n+1$ leaves

- Each algorithm output needs at least one leaf.
- A search has $n$ possible positions for the key plus the case where it is absent, so it needs at least $n+1$ leaves.
- Counting leaves is the first step in the lower-bound argument.

quiz_questions.question_text: Explain briefly why the decision tree argument shows that any worst-case comparison search needs $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons.
quiz_questions.explanation:
## Answer outline

The argument chains three facts: leaves, path length, and the leaf bound for a binary tree. Together they give the worst-case lower bound on comparisons.
concepts_tested: running time at least number of comparisons
quiz_questions.sample_answer: A comparison search must have at least $n+1$ leaves, and each root-to-leaf path is one execution whose length is at most the number of comparisons. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $2^h \geq n+1$ gives $h \geq \lceil \lg(n+1) \rceil - 1 = \Omega(\log n)$.
key_points: The tree needs at least $n+1$ leaves, one per output.
Path length equals the number of comparisons on that execution.
A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $h = \Omega(\log n)$.
